<p class="theme-lead">Designing a good optimisation algorithm usually takes experts years of trial and error, and the result rarely transfers to new problems. My research uses <b>machine learning</b> to automate this: learning <b>which search operator to apply</b>, <b>where to search</b>, <b>how to start</b>, and ultimately <b>generating whole algorithms</b> automatically.</p>

<a name="introduction"></a>
<h2>Introduction</h2>
<h3>Learning inside the optimiser</h3>
<p>Every metaheuristic is built from components — how to initialise, which operator to apply, which neighbourhood to search, when to accept a move. Each is a decision that machine learning can make better than a fixed hand-designed choice, by learning from experience on many problem instances.</p>

<h3>Two complementary learners</h3>
<p><b>Deep and reinforcement learning</b> learn flexible policies from data, while <b>genetic programming</b> learns compact, interpretable components. We study both and how they combine.</p>

<h2>My Contributions</h2>
<p>With my students and collaborators, I have made the following contributions. The papers shown are selected automatically: award-winning papers, papers with 100+ citations, and papers in top venues. Click a title to read the paper, or <i>list entry</i> to see it in my publication list.</p>

<h3 class="theme-sub"><span class="theme-sub__num">1</span> Adaptive operator selection</h3>
<p>Which operator works best changes during the search and across instances. We learn operator selectors from both offline and online experience, and surveyed the field.</p>

<h3 class="theme-sub"><span class="theme-sub__num">3</span> Automated design of algorithm components</h3>
